extracted.intended_audience: patent owners and practitioners (young lawyers & agents) preparing Patent Owner Preliminary Responses (POPRs) and Patent Owner Responses (PORs) in PTAB IPR proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing Patent Owner Preliminary Responses and Patent Owner Responses in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) proceedings, including what to include, timing, evidentiary practices, and procedural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: POPR scope (37 CFR § 42.107(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner may file a preliminary response to the petition. The response is limited to setting forth the reasons why no inter partes review should be instituted under 35 U.S.C. 314 and can include supporting evidence. The preliminary response is subject to the word count under § 42.24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional, not mandatory — “may file”. Can include supporting evidence such as new declarations, deposition transcripts, trial transcripts, expert reports, etc. Use to present institution-stage arguments aimed at defeating institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: POPR due date and waiver (37 CFR § 42.107(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary response must be filed no later than three months after the date of a notice indicating that the request to institute an inter partes review has been granted a filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due 3 months after PTAB assigns a filing date to the petition. The patent owner may expedite the proceeding by filing an election to waive the patent owner preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: No amendments at POPR stage; statutory disclaimer allowed (37 CFR § 42.107(d),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary response shall not include any amendment. The patent owner may file a statutory disclaimer under 35 U.S.C. 253(a) in compliance with § 1.321(a); disclaimed claims will not be the basis for institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment is not available at the POPR stage. A statutory disclaimer can be a powerful tool to eliminate grounds or defeat the entire petition by removing claims at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional challenges to raise in POPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential jurisdiction challenges include whether the petitioner met the 1-year statutory bar, whether a declaratory judgment complaint was filed prior to the petition, real party in interest/privity issues (estoppel), and whether the petition named all real parties in interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POPR is an appropriate stage to raise threshold jurisdictional defects that can prevent institution (timing/statutory bar, DJ suit precedence, RPI/privity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary and claim-construction challenges to raise in POPR
rubrics_metrics.description: POPR can raise claim construction challenges and discretionary bases for denial of institution such as parallel district court litigation, multiple petitions, and § 325(d) ‘substantially the same art or arguments.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus institution-stage briefing on reasons under § 314(a) and § 325(d) that the Board should use its discretion to deny institution; emphasize parallels with district-court proceedings and duplication of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: POR scope and filing timing (37 CFR § 42.120(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may file a single response to the petition and/or decision on institution. A patent owner response is filed as an opposition, is subject to page/word limits under § 42.24, and if no date is provided, the default filing date is three months from the date the inter partes review was instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word count: 14,000 words. Generally due 3 months after institution but always check the scheduling order because the Board may set a shorter period.

rubrics_metrics.name: POR content guidance — include all arguments for Final Written Decision (FWD)
rubrics_metrics.description: POR must include all arguments that will inform the Final Written Decision. POR arguments are often much more factual and should be framed to support the FWD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel toward use of figures (particularly in POR). Because motions to amend are generally contingent, a POR should make the best substantive case now even if an amendment is also filed. POR should assemble factual record and evidence (depositions, expert declarations) to support defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive arguments to raise in POR
rubrics_metrics.description: Common substantive challenges include missing claim elements, claim construction disputes, status of references as prior art, anticipation arguments (including inherency), and obviousness arguments (show motivation to combine, sufficient explanation, and address secondary indicia of non-obviousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POR should comprehensively address anticipation and obviousness theories — attack motivation, reasoning, and present affirmative evidence of non-obviousness (secondary indicia). Use factual development and expert support where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word limits for POPR, POR, and sur-reply (§ 42.24; sur-reply guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: POPR and POR are subject to the same word limit: 14,000 words (IPR). Sur-reply word limit is 5,600 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically there were page limits; current practice uses word counts. Plan arguments and use figures to conserve word count, especially in POR. Sur-replies are shorter and narrowly responsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sur-reply rules (37 CFR § 42.23(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A sur-reply may only respond to arguments raised in the corresponding reply and may not be accompanied by new evidence other than deposition transcripts of the cross-examination of any reply witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sur-reply to petitioner’s reply is now a matter of right. Do not introduce new evidence in a sur-reply except deposition transcripts of cross-examination; plan to put substantive evidence into earlier filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replies to POPRs — Board permission standard (37 CFR § 42.108(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Replies to Patent Owner Preliminary Responses can be requested from the Board but must be accompanied by a showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner should demonstrate good cause to obtain leave to file a reply to a POPR; otherwise replies are not automatic at the POPR stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition timing and notice for POR support (37 CFR § 42.53(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition intended to support the POR must take place more than a week before filing the POR. The party seeking the deposition must file a notice of deposition at least ten days before the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule depositions early to allow incorporation into POR (and for potential cross-examination transcripts to be used in sur-replies). Goals of depositions: obtain key admissions, clarify confusing testimony, and cut off future counter-arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting evidence and expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporting declarations from one or more experts and supportive evidence (textbooks, prior proceedings transcripts, expert reports) can be very impactful but the owner must 'know the whole reference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert declarations and documentary evidence to bolster factual and technical points; thoroughly vet prior-art references and secondary-evidence sources to anticipate petitioner counter-arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations and next steps (practical timing of PTAB stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical timeline elements and strategy considerations (e.g., POPR vs POR timing, discovery, depositions, replies, motions to amend, and appeal availability) guide how to allocate work and evidence gathering across the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start evidence gathering early. Recognize that POPR is not part of trial record (so may need to remake arguments in POR). POR often requires more factual development (discovery, depositions). Petitioner gets a reply; appeals remain available after final decisions.
